## Before You Start {#before-you-start}

::: {.callout-important title="The CUNEF server at a glance"}
The CUNEF compute server is reachable at `naranjito.cunef.edu`. It is a single large machine running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, with two **Intel Xeon 6740E** CPUs (**192 cores** in total), **256 GB of RAM** (about 212 GB schedulable), and **four NVIDIA L40S GPUs** (48 GB each), all shared by everyone through the Slurm scheduler. You log in, prepare your code and environment, and then ask Slurm to run the work through `sbatch` or `srun`. [Section 1.6](server.qmd#partitions) lists the full hardware.
:::

A handful of names and terms recur throughout this guide. The table below is a quick glossary.

| Value | What it is |
|:----------|:-------------------------------|
| `naranjito.cunef.edu` | The hostname you connect to (by SSH, VS Code, or browser). |
| `<username>` | Your CUNEF server user name. Replace it wherever it appears below. |
| Partitions | `general` (batch jobs), `interactive`, `preemptible`: the Slurm queues you can submit to ([Section 1.6](server.qmd#partitions)). The older `short` and `long` still exist so that existing scripts keep working. |
| Usage limits | How much of the server each user can hold, and for how long ([Section 1.7](server.qmd#usage-limits)). |
| Hardware | One shared node: 192 CPU cores, 256 GB RAM, and 4 NVIDIA L40S GPUs ([Section 1.6](server.qmd#partitions)). |
| `$HOME` | Your personal directory for code, scripts, and Conda environments. |

**What Slurm, `sbatch`, and `srun` are.** Because `naranjito` is shared by many people at once, you do not start heavy programs on it directly. Instead a scheduler called *Slurm* hands out the machine's cores, memory, and GPUs fairly. You write a short description of the work you want done (e.g. how long it should run and how many resources it needs) and submit it to Slurm, which queues the request and starts it as soon as room is free. You submit in one of two ways: `sbatch` runs a script unattended in the background (the usual choice), while `srun` opens a live interactive session on the resources it grants you. Almost everything in this guide is about writing and submitting those job descriptions.

::: {.callout-note title="Rule of thumb"}
Use a plain login shell for editing files, installing small packages, moving data, and submitting jobs. Run real computation (models, simulations, notebooks, anything that uses serious CPU, RAM, or GPU time) through `sbatch` or `srun` so the scheduler can manage it. Do not launch heavy programs directly on the login shell.
:::
